Ibn Kathir rapporte aussi que la Tradition sur la permission de découvrir les cheveux ou la tête ne fait pas l'unanimité, et qu'al-Qurtubi juge que la femme âgée est en principe soumise à la même pudeur que la jeune, hormis le jilbab.

Ibn 'Ashur, al-Sha'rawi et Ibn 'Uthaymin soulignent que cette permission suppose l'absence de risque de tentation. Ibn 'Uthaymin ajoute que le jugement suit sa raison d'être et que le plus sûr est de s'éloigner de ce qui peut éveiller le soupçon.

Ce verset lève la gêne qui pesait sur l'aveugle, le boiteux et le malade : aucun blâme ne leur est imputé pour ce que leur infirmité les empêche de faire. Il permet aux croyants de manger dans les maisons de leurs enfants, de leurs parents, de leurs frères et sœurs, de leurs oncles et tantes paternels et maternels, dans celles qu'ils gardent par mandat, ou chez leurs amis. Selon al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et al-Baghawi, la levée du blâme concerne la commensalité : certains musulmans évitaient de manger avec ces personnes, ou craignaient de manger le bien d'autrui en leur absence. Al-Razi et al-Qurtubi rapportent les différents avis sur les causes de la révélation, et al-Tabari juge préférable de s'en tenir au sens apparent du texte sans trancher un récit précis. Le passage « manger ensemble ou séparément » ne pose pas de blâme, bien que plusieurs commentateurs, dont Ibn Kathir, notent que manger en groupe est plus béni. Quant au salut, la plupart des exégètes, dont al-Tabari et Ibn Juzayy, comprennent que lorsqu'on entre dans une maison, on salue ses occupants ; s'il n'y a personne, on dit : « Que la paix soit sur nous et sur les serviteurs pieux d'Allah ». Ibn Kathir et al-Alusi rappellent que cette salutation vient d'Allah, qu'elle est bénie et bonne. Ibn Juzayy et al-Qasimi soulignent qu'elle apporte la paix et les bienfaits.

Ce verset définit les vrais croyants comme ceux qui, lorsqu'ils se trouvent avec le Prophète ﷺ pour une affaire commune, comme le combat, la prière du vendredi ou une consultation générale, ne le quittent pas sans l'avoir demandé. S'ils sollicitent sa permission pour une raison valable, il peut l'accorder à qui il veut, et Dieu leur pardonne. Al-Tabari et Ibn Kathir y voient une règle de bonne conduite envers le chef de la communauté, et Ibn Kathir précise que celui qui s'y conforme compte parmi les croyants accomplis. Sur le sens de « affaire commune », les avis se répartissent : pour Ibn Zayd et Ibn Salam, il s'agit surtout du combat ou de la prière avec sermon, alors qu'al-Tabari, Ibn Jawzi et d'autres l'entendent de toute obéissance collective. Al-Zamakhshari et al-Razi insistent sur la gravité de partir sans permission, qui relève de l'hypocrisie, tandis qu'al-Baydawi souligne que la demande de permission est un signe de foi. Quant au pouvoir d'accorder ou de refuser, il est laissé à l'appréciation du Prophète selon l'intérêt public. Selon Qatada, ce passage a été abrogé par un verset de la sourate al-Tawba, mais d'autres commentateurs ne le suivent pas. Ibn al-Arabi, cité par al-Qurtubi, limite la règle à la guerre, alors que l'auteur retient la portée générale. Enfin, plusieurs exégètes rattachent la suite du verset à l'interdiction d'appeler le Prophète par son seul prénom et au blâme de ceux qui quittent l'assemblée en se dissimulant.

Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset enseigne aux croyants le respect dû au Prophète ﷺ, tant dans l'appel que dans la permission de quitter une assemblée. Le sens le plus partagé est que Dieu interdit de l'interpeller comme on interpelle un compagnon, par exemple « ô Muhammad », et prescrit de dire « ô Prophète de Dieu » ou « ô Messager de Dieu », avec douceur et déférence. Ibn 'Abbas, rapporté par al-Tabari, comprend plutôt que les croyants doivent craindre sa malédiction, car son invocation est exaucée. Al-Tabari retient l'explication d'Ibn 'Abbas, car les versets voisins traitent du départ sans permission et de la menace qui s'ensuit.

Les commentateurs s'accordent à identifier ceux qui se faufilent en se cachant les uns derrière les autres comme des hypocrites qui sortent discrètement de l'assemblée. Selon les récits, cela se produisait lors du prêche du vendredi, pendant le creusement du fossé, ou au combat, Mujahid parlant alors de la fuite hors des rangs. Al-Farra' et al-Zajjaj expliquent que le mot lawadh signifie se dissimuler.

Quant à l'expression « qu'ils prennent garde à ceux qui transgressent son ordre », Ibn Kathir et d'autres y voient l'ordre de Dieu ou celui du Prophète, tandis qu'al-Akhfash considère « 'an » comme superflu et que d'autres y lisent l'idée de détournement. Pour la fitna, Ibn 'Abbas l'entend comme la mort, Mujahid comme une épreuve en ce monde, al-Suddi comme l'incroyance, et al-Hasan comme la manifestation de l'hypocrisie. Le châtiment douloureux est situé par les uns dans ce monde, par les autres dans l'au-delà.

Les juristes ont tiré de ce passage que l'ordre implique l'obligation, car Dieu menace celui qui le transgresse. D'autres exégètes, comme Ibn 'Ashur, préfèrent voir dans le mot amr le sens d'affaire ou de conduite, ce qui change la portée de l'argument.

Ce verset conclut la sourate en rappelant que tout ce qui est dans les cieux et sur la terre appartient à Dieu seul, qu'Il connaît la condition des hommes, qu'elle soit apparente ou secrète, qu'il s'agisse de foi, d'hypocrisie, d'obéissance ou de désobéissance, et qu'au jour du retour vers Lui, Il leur fera connaître leurs actes et les rétribuera, car Il est omniscient. La plupart des exégètes y voient un avertissement sur la royauté et la science divines, qui doivent conduire à craindre de désobéir à Ses ordres. Tous s'accordent à dire que le retour à Dieu désigne le Jour de la Résurrection. En revanche, ils divergent sur le destinataire : al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et al-Baghawi élargissent le propos à tous les hommes, tandis qu'al-Razi, al-Nasafi, Ibn Juzayy et al-Bayd̲awi estiment que « le jour où ils retournent » vise les hypocrites, ou qu'il y a un tournant du discours vers eux. La plupart considèrent que « qad » ici marque la certitude et renforce la menace, al-Zamakhshari expliquant qu'elle renforce le sens de la menace ; Ibn Uthaymin la tient aussi pour une affirmation, tandis que les deux Jalal notent qu'elle peut parfois indiquer la faiblesse. Ibn 'Ashur voit dans le verset une conclusion générale à toute la sourate, et précise que « ce que vous êtes » englobe les états bons et mauvais. Ibn Kathir souligne que l'annonce divine porte sur les petites comme sur les grandes actions. Les commentaires concordent pour dire que l'expression « ce que vous êtes » comprend la foi, l'hypocrisie, l'obéissance et la désobéissance, certains la limitant à l'hypocrisie dans ce contexte. Le sens commun qui se dégage est donc que Dieu possède tout, sait tout, et demandera compte à Ses serviteurs au Jour de la Résurrection.
en: This opening verse honours the sura by stating that God sent it down, imposed its rulings and placed in it clear signs so that believers may remember and act upon them. The commentators agree that the sura is Medinan, and al-Qurtubi notes that its main purpose is to regulate chastity and modesty; he also cites a letter of Umar asking the people of Kufa to teach their women this sura. The commentators differ on the reading "farradnaha" with the doubled letter. Ibn Abbas and Mujahid take it to mean that God explained and clarified the sura, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi understand the intensified form as conveying emphasis on the obligation or the multitude of duties it contains. Al-Tabari judges both readings correct, since God both detailed the sura and imposed obligations in it. As for the "clear signs", Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan take them to be the admonitions, rulings and examples in the sura free of ambiguity, whereas Mujahid sees in them the lawful and the unlawful, and al-Razi notes that they may also include proofs of God's oneness. Al-Biqa'i and al-Baydawi connect the verse with the preceding sura and see the purpose of the signs as leading people to reflection and righteousness. The detailed rulings on fornication, false accusation and mutual oath-swearing between spouses follow in the passage that comes next.

This verse sets the punishment for the unmarried fornicating man and woman, both free and virgin: one hundred lashes each. According to most scholars, the Sunna adds a one-year exile. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report from Ibn Umar, Ata, Mujahid and Qatada that the prohibition of compassion means not suspending or lightening the punishment, and that the blows should hurt without causing lasting injury. Said ibn al-Musayyab and al-Hasan understood it as striking firmly while still causing pain. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that the blows should spare the face, head and sensitive parts, and that the punishment is carried out before the authorities. On how many witnesses should attend, opinions differ: one or more according to Mujahid and Ibn Abbas, two according to Ata and Ikrima, three according to az-Zuhri and Qatada, four according to Malik and ash-Shafii by analogy with the witnesses to adultery, and ten according to al-Hasan. At-Tabari concludes that one suffices in principle, but recommends at least four. The commentators also explain that prostitution was open in that period, and that some Muslims wished to marry prostitutes, which led to the following verse on marriage. Scholars disagree on whether the prohibition concerns intercourse or the contract itself, and some hold it was abrogated by the verse on marrying the single. As for stoning for the married offender, it rests on the widely transmitted Sunna; scholars differ on whether it is combined with the lashes, with Ahmad, Ishaq and Ali allowing both, while the majority limit it to stoning alone.

This verse states that a fornicator generally marries only a fornicatrix or an idolatress, and a fornicatrix is generally married only by a fornicator or an idolater, and that this is forbidden to believers. The commentators differ on the meaning of nikah here. Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak take it as intercourse, so that a fornicator has intercourse only with a fornicatrix or an idolatress; al-Tabari adopts this reading, pointing out that the verse was revealed about idolatrous prostitutes who displayed banners. Others take it as marriage in the contractual sense, relying on the occasion of revelation: poor Muslims wished to marry wealthy prostitutes who would support them, and the story of Marthad ibn Abi Marthad and 'Anaq is cited. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and others, including al-Shafi'i, hold the ruling abrogated by the verse 'marry the single among you', while Ibn al-Qayyim regards it as still in force. Al-Hasan restricts it to people already punished for fornication, and Ibn 'Ashur sees it as addressing habitual fornicators rather than a believer who slips. On whether a chaste man may marry a woman who has committed fornication, the scholars differ: al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa allow it, while Ahmad forbids it until repentance. In any case the verse warns believers away from such unions for the wrongs they involve.

This verse prescribes the punishment for accusing chaste women of unlawful intercourse without producing four witnesses: eighty lashes, their testimony is never again accepted, and they are called defiant transgressors. The commentators read the word "ramy" as slander of zina. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi note that the rule concerns free, believing, chaste women, that men are included by meaning, and that a slave receives half the punishment according to the majority, while Ibn Mas'ud and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz hold for eighty. The most debated point is the exception "except those who repent". Al-Shafi'i, Malik, Ahmad and most exegetes hold that repentance lifts the defiance and restores acceptance of testimony. Abu Hanifa, Shurayh, al-Nakha'i and Sa'id ibn Jubayr hold that the exception concerns only the label of defiance, so testimony stays rejected forever. Umar, in the case of Abu Bakra, required a retraction, whereas al-Tabari and Malik count sincere reform and remorse. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi agree that the lashes are not removed by repentance, but differ on whether the right belongs to God (Abu Hanifa) or to the victim (Malik and al-Shafi'i).

This passage sets the penalty for one who accuses chaste women of adultery without producing four witnesses: eighty lashes, a permanent bar from giving testimony, and the label of wrongdoer. The exception that follows concerns those who repent afterwards and mend their conduct: God is then forgiving and merciful toward them. The commentators differ on the scope of this exception. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy hold that it applies both to the label of wrongdoer and to the rejection of testimony, so the repentant accuser's testimony is accepted; al-Tabari explains that repentance consists of regret, abandoning the sin and good conduct. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and others report that some require the accuser to retract his accusation. Abu Hanifa, Shurayh, al-Nakha'i and al-Hasan limit the exception to the label of wrongdoer, so his testimony remains rejected forever even after repentance. Al-Sha'bi and al-Dahhak accept his testimony only after he admits to having lied. All agree that repentance does not lift the lashes and that the accusation is a major sin. Al-Tabari also notes that repentance does not cancel the accused person's right.

This verse addresses the husband who accuses his wife of adultery without having witnesses other than himself. His own oath stands in place of the four witnesses: he swears four times by Allah that he speaks the truth, and a fifth time invoking Allah's curse upon himself if he lies. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, hold that this provision is specific to spouses and that it qualifies the general ruling on slander in the preceding verse. The occasion of revelation is related with the story of Hilal ibn Umayya, while others name 'Uwaymir al-'Ajlani, and al-Qurtubi notes that the reports differ on the name though Hilal's case is the better known. According to al-Tabari and al-Zamakhshari, the wife may avert punishment by swearing four times that her husband lies, and a fifth time invoking Allah's wrath upon herself if he is truthful. Abu Hanifa, as reported by al-Razi, reads the punishment in the verse as imprisonment, whereas the majority understand it as the legal penalty. On the effect of the oath, al-Shafi'i holds that separation follows from the husband's oath alone, Abu Hanifa requires a judge's ruling, and Malik considers that it takes effect once the mutual oaths are complete. Ibn Kathir and others hold that the separation is permanent. Commentators explain that the wrath is directed at the woman because she is the source of the transgression and her denial is more likely to be false, while the curse is directed at the man. The verse ends by affirming Allah's grace and mercy, which shields the sinners from immediate punishment.

This verse concerns li'an, the oath-procedure between spouses when a husband accuses his wife of adultery and has no witnesses but himself. He swears four times by God that he speaks the truth, then in the fifth oath calls down God's curse upon himself if he is lying, and so he averts the punishment for slander. The commentators explain that the punishment averted from the wife is the punishment for adultery, and that the imprisonment mentioned by some jurists has no basis in the text. All agree that the fifth testimony contains a self-curse; the wife answers with four oaths of innocence, then calls down God's wrath upon herself if the husband is truthful. Opinions differ on when the separation takes effect: al-Shafi'i holds that it follows from the husband's oath alone, Abu Hanifa requires a judge's ruling, and Malik holds that it occurs on completion of the li'an, while most affirm a permanent prohibition of remarriage. The occasion of revelation is narrated in two forms, the story of Hilal ibn Umayya and that of 'Uwaymir al-'Ajlani, with the Hilal account generally regarded as earlier. The commentators note that the curse is assigned to the man and the wrath to the woman, for reasons relating to the gravity of the offence and the position of each party. God is oft-returning and wise, and He covers over His servants' faults.

These verses address a husband who accuses his wife of adultery without having four witnesses, so his recourse is li'an: he swears four times by God that he speaks the truth regarding what he charged her with, then in the fifth oath calls down God's curse upon himself if he is lying. If the wife does not respond, the punishment, which most commentators identify as the legal penalty for adultery, falls upon her. If she swears four times by God that he is lying, then in the fifth oath calls down God's wrath upon herself if he is truthful, that punishment is averted. The commentators agree that the punishment averted is the legal penalty, while Abu Hanifa and his followers understood it as imprisonment until she swears or confesses. Scholars differed on whether these oaths are testimonies or oaths with the wording of testimony; most held them to be emphatic oaths. Most also held that the separation is permanent, that the husband disowns the child through li'an, and that the accusation need not name the man involved, though some required it. The verse closes by noting that without God's grace and mercy, He would have hastened the punishment and exposed the liar, for God is Oft-Returning and Wise.

This verse concerns li'an, the mutual oath-taking between spouses. When a husband accuses his wife of adultery and has no witnesses but himself, he swears four times by God that he is truthful about what he says of her, and in the fifth oath he invokes God's curse upon himself if he is lying. The wife answers in the same way, swearing four times that he is a liar and, in the fifth oath, calling down God's wrath upon herself if he is telling the truth. In this way she averts the punishment. The commentators agree that the punishment averted is the prescribed hadd and not imprisonment, as the earlier mention of the punishment in the previous verse suggests. They see this provision as a mercy from God, since without it the matter would have brought immediate punishment or public disgrace.

The jurists differ on the legal consequences. Al-Shafi'i and many others, as Ibn Kathir reports, hold that the separation takes effect through the li'an itself and that the couple can never be reunited. Abu Hanifa, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad hold that separation requires the judge's ruling. They also differ on whether freedom and Islam are required of the spouses: Abu Hanifa requires them, while Malik and al-Shafi'i allow li'an between anyone whose oath is valid.

The reports of revelation chiefly concern Hilal ibn Umayya and his wife, and 'Uwaymir al-'Ajlani. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi relate the first account, while Ibn 'Ashur considers the second to be the cause and suggests the two incidents occurred close together. Ibn 'Ashur also notes that li'an is an exceptional concession for cases of necessity and should not be extended beyond them. Malik's preferred view is that it applies only when the husband claims to have seen the act or denies paternity; otherwise the hadd is imposed for slander.

This part of verse 24:10 teaches that the grace and mercy of God are what prevent Him from hastening punishment upon people and exposing their sins; He covers them and postpones their punishment out of mercy. The commentators agree that the answer to «lawla» (had it not been) is omitted and must be understood as: He would have punished you at once, or disgraced you, or inflicted upon the liar what he invoked upon himself. They note that leaving the answer out signals the enormity of the matter, so great that words cannot contain it. They agree that the verse concludes the rulings on li'an and accusing one's spouse of adultery given before it, and that the names "Tawwab" and "Hakim" mean that God accepts the repentance of one who turns back from sin and that His rulings are wise.

They differ over what the grace and mercy refer to. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others see them in the covering over of sins and the lifting of the punishment through li'an; Yahya ibn Sallam takes the grace to be Islam and the mercy to be the Qur'an; as-Suddi takes the grace to be a favour and the mercy to be a blessing. Ibn al-Jawzi and others report that the verse was revealed about Hilal ibn Umayya and his wife, while many also cite the case of Uwaymir al-Ajlani as another event, earlier or later.

Ibn Abi Safra and al-Qurtubi note that the majority view holds that the exception in the preceding verse concerns the loss of uprightness rather than the rejection of testimony in every case, and that repentance wipes away the sin.

These verses address the slander of the Prophet's wife A'isha, may God be pleased with her. The commentators explain that the 'group' refers to men from among the believers, most of whom they name as Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, Mistah ibn Uthatha, Hassan ibn Thabit and Hamna bint Jahsh. God tells the believers not to regard what befell them as pure evil, for it turned to their good: the innocence of the Truthful one was established, her rank was raised, and verses were revealed that would be recited until the Day of Resurrection. Nearly all agree that each person who spread the slander bears a share of sin in proportion to his involvement, and that the one who bore the greatest part was Ibn Ubayy, who will suffer a great punishment in the hereafter. Ibn Kathir, al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi report that Mistah, Hassan and Hamna received the legal punishment for slander, while others argue that Ibn Ubayy was not punished because he never openly accused, since the penalty requires confession or evidence. On who 'took upon himself the greater part', the majority identifies Ibn Ubayy, a view some link to A'isha herself; a minority, including reports attributed to al-Zuhri, names Hassan. Readers differ on the word 'kibrahu': the reading with a kasra is the most common, while the reading with a damma is attributed to Ya'qub and others, and philologists distinguish between 'the greater part' and 'the sin' as its meaning. From these verses the commentators draw several lessons: one must reject whoever slanders a believer without proof, avoid speaking of what one does not know, and guard the honour of believers with great seriousness.

This verse rebukes the believers for their reaction to the slander against Aisha, may God be pleased with her. God asks them why, when they heard it, the believing men and women did not think well of one another and say that this is a manifest lie. The commentators agree that the verse was revealed concerning the affair of the slander and that the particle lawla here means why not, expressing reproach and exhortation. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya report that the sense is that the believers should have judged the matter by themselves: if such a thing seems far from them, it is even further from the mother of the believers. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that the phrase 'bi-anfusihim' refers to people of their own community, since believers are like one soul, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi stress that the shift from address to third person intensifies the rebuke and reminds the believer that faith requires good assumption about a fellow believer. Al-Qurtubi and al-Razi draw from this that a believer must deny a slander against a Muslim without proof, and al-Razi adds that apparent uprightness grounds a presumption of good conduct. Ibn Ashur sees in the verse a rule that one must respond to slander about a fellow believer both in the heart and by speech. The scholars differ on the precise meaning of 'anfusihim', which some take as the mother or close relatives and others as believers in general, and on the exact function of the shift in grammatical person, which remains the main point of discussion.

This verse establishes that whoever accuses a chaste woman of adultery must produce four witnesses; if he cannot, the accusers are liars in God's judgment. It was revealed about the slander (al-ifk) against 'A'isha, the Prophet's wife. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, understand it as referring to the slanderers themselves, among them 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, Hassan ibn Thabit, Mistah and Hamna bint Jahsh. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Razi explain that "with God" means "in His judgment and law": human justice rests on outward evidence, while hidden matters belong to God. Al-Zamakhshari reads the verse as a rebuke to those who heard the slander and did not reject it, since the accuser without proof should have been denied. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya develop the point that believers should judge their brothers by putting themselves in their place. The commentators differ on who bore the greatest share of the slander: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and most others name Ibn Ubayy, while some think of Hassan. On the punishment there are different views: most hold that Hassan, Mistah and Hamna were flogged, but that Ibn Ubayy was not, a point explained either as postponing his punishment to the Hereafter or as a way of calming the discord among his people. The following verses rebuke the believers for not thinking well of their brothers.

The commentators explain that this verse addresses those who spread the slander against Aisha, and that God spared them through His grace and mercy, in this world by granting time for repentance and in the hereafter by forgiveness, otherwise a severe punishment would have befallen them for what they propagated. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi agree that the address is to the guilty among the believers, while the extent of the punishment is understood differently: some say it refers to both this world and the next. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain that God postponed the punishment, and al-Razi and al-Nasafi treat the particle "lawla" as indicating that one thing was prevented by the existence of another. Ibn Abbas and Ibn Kathir specify that the punishment of the hereafter is endless for one who does not repent, and that hypocrites such as Abd Allah ibn Ubayy have no share in this mercy. Ibn Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan discuss the various readings of the verb "talaqqawnahu", with its senses of receiving, throwing out, or lying, which shows that the blame falls on passing on rumours without knowledge. All agree that "afada fi al-hadith" means to plunge into a discussion. The commentators do not judge between the opinions but report them as they stand, and retain that this is a reminder to the believers of God's favour.

This verse rebukes those who spread the slander against Aisha, may God be pleased with her. Its plain meaning is that they received this talk from one another, each passing it on, and uttered it with their mouths without any knowledge or certainty, while considering it a light matter when it is grave in God's sight. The commentators agree that the verse censures three things: receiving and spreading the report, speaking about what one does not know, and belittling the sin. Al-Tabari, Mujahid and Ibn Kathir explain that the phrase means relating the report to one another, and al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir cite Aisha's reading with the sense of lying, while treating the common reading as the most established. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi see the mention of mouths as emphasis showing that the words did not come from a conviction of the heart, whereas Ibn Ashur links it to the clause about having no knowledge. Al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi report a disagreement over whether the Prophet applied the legal punishment to some of the slanderers, and they do not settle the question. The scholars conclude that treating a sin as minor does not lessen it but increases its gravity and makes it easier to repeat.

This passage rebukes the believers for not rejecting the slander the moment they heard it; they should have said at once that such talk was not becoming for them, and glorified God, who cannot allow such a thing to touch the household of His Prophet. The commentators agree that the verse concerns the slander against 'A'isha, may God be pleased with her. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di read 'subhanaka' as a glorification of God, exalted above such lies, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Nasafi stress that it expresses wonder at the enormity of the charge. Al-Razi lists several reasons why silence and rejection were required, including the harm done to the Prophet and his family. Ibn 'Atiyya defines slander as saying of a person what is not in him. Al-Qurtubi reports that Abu Ayyub al-Ansari and his wife spoke these words before the verse was revealed. Opinions differ on who bore the greatest share of the slander: most, including al-Tabari, Mujahid, al-Suddi and Ibn Kathir, name Abdullah ibn Ubayy, while others, relying on a report from al-Sha'bi, name Hassan ibn Thabit. Scholars also disagree on punishment: al-Mawardi reports the view that no one was flogged, whereas al-Qurtubi and most scholars hold that Hassan, Mistah and Hamna were lashed. Readings of the verb 'talaqqunahu' vary between transmitting and inventing, but all these readings point to passing on news without knowledge.

The commentators explain that this verse admonishes the believers never to return to what happened during the affair of the slander, namely spreading false accusations against ʿĀ'isha without knowledge. The condition «if you are believers» is, for most of them, a way of stirring the faithful to heed the warning. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read it as a plain prohibition against repeating the offence, while al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan prefer to supply «lest» or «regarding» before the verb, which does not change the sense. Al-Razi reports that the Mu'tazilites took the verse to show that abstaining from slander is part of faith; he replies that the verse also addresses believers who took part in the affair, so it should be read as a warning meant to restrain them. Al-Qurtubi cites Malik, who held that insulting ʿĀ'isha contradicts the Quran, whereas Shafi'i scholars judged that this does not amount to unbelief. The commentators agree that the verse closes with God's knowledge and wisdom in clarifying His signs, and that heeding this admonition is a sign of sincere faith.

In this verse God explains that the admonitions and rulings given concerning the affair of the slander (al-ifk) are a clarification from Him for the believers. He sets out clearly the signs, meaning the proofs and guideposts that lead them to what is good for them, and He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise. The commentators explain these signs as the commands, prohibitions, laws and good manners. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir connect the verse to the prohibition on the believers returning to what they had done by spreading the slander about A'isha, may God be pleased with her. Ibn Zayd, quoted by al-Tabari, sees in it a favour: God made this affair known so that the believers would not fall into the same error. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi understand the signs as the clear proofs of God's knowledge and wisdom through the laws and counsels He sends down. Al-Razi argues that God's knowledge and wisdom make it necessary to accept what He makes clear, while disputing some points of this reasoning with the Mu'tazilites. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the mention of these two attributes suits the context of reminder. The commentators thus agree on the general sense of the verse, which closes the warning by affirming that God makes His rulings clear to His servants.

This verse warns that those who love to see indecency spread among the believers will face a painful punishment in this world and in the next, and reminds the reader that God knows the truth and the hidden intentions of hearts, while people only see outward things. The commentators link the verse to the slander against 'A'isha, whose chief instigator was 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that the painful punishment in this world is the prescribed hadd penalty for slander, and that the punishment in the Hereafter is the Fire; al-Tabari adds that this applies to someone who dies persisting in it without repenting. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi hold that the threat also concerns the love of spreading indecency itself, which lies in the heart, and that the punishment of the Hereafter falls on the one who both loves and spreads it. Ibn 'Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and al-Qurtubi argue the verse is general and applies to any slanderer, whether hypocrite or believer, while Mujahid and Ibn Zayd limit it to the hypocrites. Ibn Juzayy notes the difficulty of combining the hadd with a punishment in the Hereafter and offers several answers. Al-Razi observes that the verse shows that intending a grave sin is itself sinful. Opinions differ on who bore the greatest share of the calumny: most identify 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, while some name Hassan ibn Thabit. The commentators also draw lessons about thinking well of fellow believers and not spreading harmful talk, which Ibn 'Ashur develops by stressing the moral and social harm caused by rumours.

This verse states that, but for Allah's grace and mercy toward you, and because Allah is compassionate and merciful, those who spread the slander would have been punished at once. Most commentators supply an omitted answer to "law la" (had it not been), each restoring it differently: the punishment would have struck you, you would have been destroyed, or you would have been exposed. The scholars agree that these verses concern the affair of 'A'isha, the Prophet's wife, and that the "group" refers to those who spread the accusation, among them Ibn Ubayy, Hassan, Mistah and Hamna. They differ on who bore the greatest share: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most others name Ibn Ubayy, whereas some name Hassan, citing the blindness that later struck him. Al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi list several meanings of the "footsteps of Satan", including his sins, his traces, and oaths of vows made in disobedience. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Atiyya note that the threat applies in principle to every slanderer, while others limit it to hypocrites. The meaning of "zaka" is also debated: to be purified, to be guided, or to be reformed; Ibn Kathir stresses that Allah purifies whom He wills by His grace. Commentators present these passages as a lesson on the gravity of slander and on the duty to think well of fellow believers.

In this verse God commands the believers not to follow the steps of Satan, meaning his paths, his whispers and his enticements to sin. Whoever follows them ends up committing indecency and wrongdoing, because Satan commands both. Commentators explain the 'steps' in various ways: Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and 'Ikrima take them as his deeds and promptings, Abu Mijlaz includes vows made in disobedience, and others understand them as moving from the lawful to the forbidden. Most link the verset to the slander against 'A'isha, saying that spreading indecency is one of these steps. On the phrase 'had it not been for God's grace and mercy, none of you would ever have been purified', al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand that no one would have been righteous or cleansed of sin, while al-Tabari and al-Zamakhshari stress that repentance, which erases sin, is what is meant. Ibn Zayd takes purification here to mean Islam, and some apply the verse to all people while others restrict it to the slanderers. The reading with doubled letters stresses that purification comes from God's favour alone. God hears what they say and knows their intentions, which urges sincerity in repentance. Several scholars also note that worldly judgments follow outward appearances, while inner intentions belong to God.

The commentators explain that the verse forbids the people of virtue and means among the believers from swearing to withhold their kindness from their kin, the needy and the emigrants in God's path, and urges them to pardon and overlook, reminding them that they themselves wish to be forgiven by God. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Razi and al-Baghawi largely agree that it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, who had sworn not to spend on Mistah ibn Uthatha, his maternal cousin, after Mistah took part in the slander against A'isha; Abu Bakr then resumed his support when he heard the verse. Al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya also cite another report, from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak, that several believers had cut off their benefits to all who had spoken of the affair; Ibn 'Atiyya prefers the first report while holding that the verse's meaning extends to everyone. On the verb ya'tali, most take it as meaning to swear, while Abu 'Ubayda, Abu Muslim and al-Zamakhshari take it as meaning to fall short or to spare no effort. Al-Qurtubi and al-Razi draw from it that swearing to abandon good is blameworthy, and that one who has sworn and then sees a better course should take it and make expiation, the view of most jurists. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Qasimi highlight the moral lesson of mutual forgiveness between God and people.

This verse states that those who accuse chaste, unsuspecting, believing women of adultery are cursed in this world and the next, and that a great punishment awaits them. The commentators agree that the wording is general and applies to anyone who accuses a woman with these qualities, though they differ on the occasion of revelation and on its scope. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and, in one report, Ibn Abbas say it refers specifically to 'A'isha, but al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi favour a general application, al-Tabari holding that the ruling covers every woman with these qualities. Al-Dahhak, Abu al-Jawza' and others say it refers to the wives of the Prophet, for whom no repentance is accepted, while those who accuse other believing women may repent, as the following verse indicates. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Tabari hold that the threat depends on the absence of repentance. Al-Razi discusses whether the accuser becomes an unbeliever and concludes that the general reading is the sound one. Al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi explain the curse as lashes, social exclusion and loss of trustworthiness. Most commentators note that the tongues, hands and feet of the accusers will testify against them on the Day of Judgement, with disagreement between Sunni and Mu'tazili scholars on how this testimony works. Ibn Kathir and others add that the verse magnifies the gravity of the slander against the believers.

This verse describes the punishment of those who accuse chaste, heedless, believing women of adultery: they are cursed in this world and the next and face a great torment. On the Day when their tongues, hands and feet testify against them about what they did, God will repay them their due, and they will then know that God is the manifest Truth. The commentators agree in linking the passage to the slander against Aisha, may God be pleased with her, and that the limbs will testify against their owners.

They differ, however, on the scope of the warning. Ibn Abbas in one report, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Muqatil take it to refer specifically to Aisha's accusers or to Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his followers. Al-Tabari and most scholars, including Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya, read it as general, applying to anyone who slanders a believing, chaste woman, with Aisha as the occasion of revelation. Al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi restrict it to the wives of the Prophet. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi report that the Mu'tazilites read the testimony of the limbs as God creating speech in them, whereas the Sunni tradition keeps it in its apparent sense. Ibn Ashur notes that the verse primarily targets Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions among the hypocrites.

The commentators also agree that God makes the limbs speak on the Day of Judgment, though they differ on how that speech occurs. Slandering chaste women is regarded as a grave sin.

This verse says that on the Day of Judgment, when their tongues, hands and feet testify against them for what they did, God will repay people in full and with justice, and that the disbelievers and hypocrites will then know with certainty that God is the Manifest Truth. The commentators explain that the word din here means recompense or reckoning, and that al-haqq describes that recompense as just. Mujahid read the word in the nominative, making it an attribute of God, a reading the majority of reciters did not adopt and that al-Tabari and others count among the irregular readings. Ibn Abbas said the verse refers to Abdullah ibn Ubayy, who doubted the religion and would come to know the truth then. On its scope, Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari hold that it applies to anyone who slanders a chaste believing woman, with the Prophet's wives and especially Aisha being most included. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Muqatil say it refers to Aisha alone, while al-Dahhak says it refers only to the Prophet's wives. On repentance, most exegetes make forgiveness conditional on not repenting, whereas a report attributed to Ibn Abbas denies repentance to those who spread the slander against Aisha. Al-Razi and Ibn Atiyya note that mentioning the body parts' testimony stresses the gravity of the act.

This verse states that impure words and deeds suit impure people, men and women, while pure words and deeds suit pure people, so each kind is joined to its like. The commentators link the passage to the slander episode (al-ifk) and read it as an acquittal of Aisha and Safwan ibn al-Mu'attal. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Qatada and most exegetes take the impure and pure things to be words: impure speech belongs to impure people and pure speech to pure people. Al-Tabari prefers this reading because the preceding verses concern the slanderers. Ibn Zayd understands men and women instead: impure women for impure men and pure women for pure men. Ibn Kathir also records this view and reasons that a wife of the Prophet, the purest of men, could not be impure. On the phrase 'these are cleared of what they say', al-Farra' takes Aisha and Safwan as the referents, using the plural as in the verse on brothers, while others apply it to the pure generally. All agree the promise is forgiveness and generous provision, which commentators identify with the Garden. As for the curse on those who accuse chaste women, some restrict it to the Prophet's wives, while others extend it to all believing women, with the Prophet's wives included first and foremost.

This verse forbids believers from entering houses other than their own without seeking permission and greeting the occupants. Most commentators understand the word "tasta'nisu" to mean seeking permission. Al-Tabari and others report that some readers recited it as "tasta'dhinu", while Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Alusi and Ibn Kathir reject the report attributed to Ibn 'Abbas that the word was a scribal error, and hold the known reading to be correct. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi also take it to mean making oneself known or ascertaining the situation, so that the occupant knows of the visitor. On the order of greeting and asking permission, scholars differ: some give priority to asking permission following the literal wording, the majority say one greets first and then asks, and others distinguish according to whether the visitor sees the occupant. Commentators explain that permission protects privacy and what should be concealed, prevents suspicion, and spares the host embarrassment. Al-Mawardi, Ibn Kathir and al-Nawawi report that one asks three times and withdraws if not admitted, following the account of Abu Musa with 'Umar. For the following verse, most commentators distinguish inhabited houses from uninhabited places such as inns, shops or lodgings, which may be entered without asking because they serve a legitimate purpose, though they differ on how to identify them. The verse closes by reminding that God knows what is shown and what is hidden, a warning against spying on homes.

The verse tells believers not to enter other people's homes without permission and to greet the occupants. If they find no one there to grant leave, they must not enter until they are given permission; if they are told to go back, they should go back, as that is purer for them. The commentators agree that the rule protects privacy and prevents seeing what people hide, and that entering another's property without consent is forbidden. Al-Tabari and Mujahid read "if you find no one in them" as "if you have no goods in them," but al-Tabari rejects this because Arabs do not use "anyone" for objects. Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "tastadhinu" (ask permission) rather than "tasta'nisu", while al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya keep the sense of seeking to know who is inside. Scholars differ on whether to greet first or ask permission first; most say greet first, and the hadith gives the formula "Peace be upon you, may I enter?" repeated three times. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir report that turning away graciously is good manners and that one should not stand facing the door. The verse that follows allows entry without permission to buildings open to the public, such as inns and shops, with some scholars naming different buildings, and whether the verse is abrogated is disputed.

This verse says there is no blame on believers for entering uninhabited buildings without seeking permission, provided they have some benefit there. The commentators differ on what these buildings are. Qatada, Mujahid and Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya take them to be the inns and caravanserais built on travel routes, where travellers stop and store their goods; ‘Ata’ takes them to be ruined houses used for relieving oneself; Ibn Zayd and al-Sha‘bi take them to be merchants’ shops and market stalls. Ibn Jarir favours a general sense, any house without residents. As for the word matā‘ (benefit), most understand it as a use, such as shelter from heat and cold, storing goods, or buying and selling, while others read it as satisfying a need. All agree that the verse carries a warning against anyone who enters such places for corruption or to spy on what is private. Some treat it as an exception to the earlier rule requiring permission, while others see a separate ruling that does not abrogate or limit it, since permission remains required in lived-in homes. Jurists distinguish shops, for which many require the owner’s consent, and several scholars regard Ibn Zayd’s view on this point as mistaken. All agree that the greeting comes before the request to enter, and that seeking permission applies even among close relatives. The verse ends by reminding that God knows what people reveal and what they conceal.

This verse tells the Prophet ﷺ to tell the believers to lower their gaze from what is forbidden to them and to guard their private parts, for that is purer for them, and Allah is fully aware of what they do. The commentators agree that lowering the gaze means turning it away from what is unlawful, and that guarding the private parts includes abstaining from adultery and covering nakedness. On the particle "min" in "from their gazes", al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Atiyya take it as partitive, since the first accidental glance is not within one's control and is not held against a person. Al-Sam'ani and al-Baghawi, citing al-Akhfash, consider it superfluous, while Ibn al-Qayyim and others give other readings. Abu al-'Aliya and Ibn Zayd say that in this passage guarding the private parts means concealing them, whereas most scholars understand it as avoiding fornication, and al-Alusi holds that both meanings are included. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir cite hadiths about the first glance and the sudden glance. Al-Qurtubi discusses the rules of the public bath, and Ibn Kathir and al-Shawkani address women, slaves and male attendants lacking desire. On the visible adornment, Ibn Mas'ud says it is the garments, Ibn Abbas says kohl and the ring, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Awza'i say the face and hands. All agree that modesty is required of women, and many accept leniency for what is hard to cover, such as the face and hands. The verse is read as a set of safeguards against temptation, since the gaze is the messenger of desire.

This verse teaches believing women modesty and restraint: to lower their gaze from what is not lawful, to guard their private parts, not to display their adornment except what appears of its own accord, and to draw their head coverings over their chests. The commentators agree that hidden adornment, such as jewellery, necklaces and anklets, may be shown only to those the verse names: husbands, fathers, sons, brothers, their sons, sisters' sons, other believing women, those whom the right hand possesses, male attendants without desire, and young children who do not yet know the intimate matters of women. They link this list to kinship and to the need for regular contact.

Opinions differ on what the apparent adornment is. Ibn Mas'ud took it to be clothing, while Ibn Abbas and Qatada named kohl, rings and henna, and al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Ata' spoke of the face and hands. Al-Tabari concluded that the soundest view is the face and palms, since women uncover these in prayer, and he included kohl, rings and henna within that. Ibn al-'Arabi held that a woman must conceal as much as she can, and that the exception applies only to what necessity makes impossible to cover.

Scholars also disagreed about slaves and eunuchs. Ibn Abbas allowed a male slave to see his mistress's hair, Ibn al-Musayyab restricted the verse to female slaves, and Abu Hanifa treated a male slave as a stranger. Al-Qurtubi and others note that the verse forbids striking the feet to make ankle bracelets audible, a sign that whatever stirs desire must be avoided. The verse ends by calling all believers to repent together in hope of success.

The verse tells the guardians and masters to marry off the unmarried men and women, whether widowed or never married, as well as the righteous male and female slaves. Most commentators, including al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, read the command as a recommendation, while the Zahiris, as al-Razi reports, read it as an obligation; al-Razi himself concludes it is recommended. As for the phrase that if they are poor God will enrich them out of His bounty, Ibn Mas'ud, Umar and Abu Bakr take it as a promise of wealth for those who marry, whereas al-Mawardi and al-Razi regard it as conditional on God's will, citing the parallel verse in Surat al-Tawba. Al-Baydawi and al-Razi note that marriage does not always bring wealth, and Ibn Juzayy sees the verse as encouragement to marry in pursuit of God's pleasure. On compelling a master to marry his slave, al-Shafi'i accepts it, while Malik rejects it in some cases, and Ibn Kathir reports the divergent views. Regarding the written manumission contract (mukatabah), Ata' and Dawud hold it obligatory when the slave asks and shows good conduct, while the majority consider it recommended; the scholars differ on what 'good' means, whether wealth, earning capacity, honesty or piety. Finally the verse forbids compelling slave girls into prostitution, a practice that al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir link to the case of Abd Allah ibn Ubayy.

The commentators explain that this verse addresses three matters linked to chastity, marriage and the rights of slaves. First, it orders guardians and masters to marry off the unmarried free people and the righteous slaves, and poverty should not prevent this, for God will enrich them from His bounty, as al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir state. Whoever cannot marry should seek chastity; al-Shafi'i and Ibn Kathir understand this as patience and fasting, while al-Tabari takes marriage to mean the ability to pay the dowry, and al-Razi and al-Qurtubi advise the one without means to remain chaste. Second comes the mukatabah, a contract by which a slave buys his freedom with a sum paid in instalments. The commentators broadly agree that when the slave asks for it and his master recognises in him good character and an ability to earn, it is recommended according to the majority, including Malik, al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa, whereas Ata', Amr ibn Dinar and the Zahiris hold it obligatory, a view al-Tabari prefers. They differ on what the 'good' means: Ibn Abbas and Mujahid take it as wealth, Ibn Umar and al-Shafi'i as the ability to earn together with honesty, and al-Hasan as religious commitment. As for remitting part of the sum, Ali suggests a quarter, Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan a third, Qatada a tenth, and Malik sets no measure. Third, masters are forbidden to force their slave-women into prostitution when they wish to remain chaste; the commentators report that the verse was revealed concerning the slave-women of Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, and Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari hold that one who is coerced bears no sin. Al-Zamakhshari reads the condition as describing the usual reality rather than a limit. God knows best what He intends.

The commentators explain that God sent down in this sura clear verses that distinguish truth from falsehood and set out the rulings and legal limits, together with an example, meaning a striking account of earlier peoples from which lessons may be drawn, and an admonition that benefits the God-fearing in particular. Their shared reading is that the verses are clear in themselves, and that stories like those of Joseph and Mary, and the affair of 'A'isha, which some link to the occasion of revelation, show that slander and injustice are ancient and that the outcome favours innocence and piety. Most agree that the admonition is for the pious, who alone benefit from it, even though it is addressed in general. They differ on the recitation: most readers read 'mubayyanat' with a fatha, meaning God made them clear, while others read it with a kasra, meaning they make the truth clear; al-Tabari judges the two readings close in meaning and both correct. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi note that the kasra may mean 'became clear', as in the proverb 'the dawn has become clear to the one with two eyes'. As for the example, al-Dahhak takes it to mean the prescriptions of the Torah and the Gospel, Muqatil the punishment inflicted on those who denied the messengers, and others a remarkable story from earlier nations.

The commentators explain that God is the light of the heavens and the earth, and Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and others take this to mean the guide of their inhabitants or the one who illumines them, while Mujahid takes it as the one who governs their affairs and Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Abu al-'Aliya as the one who adorns them. They agree that the light attributed to Him carries the sense of guidance and clarity, and that the Qur'anic verses are a light from Him. As for 'the likeness of His light', they differ over what it refers to: Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid take it as God's own light or His guidance in the believer's heart, Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn Jubayr as the believer's light, Ka'b al-Ahbar and al-Dahhak as the light of the Prophet, and al-Hasan and Zayd ibn Aslam as the Qur'an. The niche (mishkah) is for most a non-piercing recess in a wall, while others take it to be the place of the wick in the lamp or the iron hook that holds it; the lamp (misbah) is the flame and the glass the globe around it. All agree the oil comes from a blessed olive tree that almost lights up by itself, yet they differ on its position: Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima and Qatada say it is exposed to the sun all day; al-Hasan says it is not a tree of this world; Ibn Zayd says it grows in Syria. The readings differ on the word durriyy and on the verb yuqadu. They conclude that guidance belongs to God alone, that the parables are given so people may understand, and that God knows all things.

The commentators explain that this verse describes houses which God has permitted to be raised and honoured, most often understood as mosques, where His name is remembered and where He is glorified morning and evening. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi note that raising these houses means building them, honouring them and keeping them clean of idle talk and impurities, while the remembrance covers recitation of the Book, prayer and other acts of worship. Ibn 'Abbas takes the morning and evening to mean the dawn and afternoon prayers, and most exegetes see them as the obligatory prayers, though others hold that the glorification is broader than prayer alone. The commentators agree that the men described are believers whom neither trade nor sale distracts from the remembrance of God, from prayer and from almsgiving, and that their fear of a day when hearts and eyes will be turned about moves them to this. Al-Tabari reports that Ibn 'Umar, Salim ibn 'Abd Allah and Ibn Mas'ud saw merchants leave their stalls at the call to prayer and identified them with the verse. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir explain that the reward is for their best deeds, with extra grace added, and that provision without reckoning expresses abundance. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan note that trade may mean buying or importing goods, with selling mentioned afterwards for emphasis. Some have also held that the houses are the homes of the prophets, Bayt al-Maqdis or all houses, but most retain the mosques because of the mention of glorification.

This verse describes men who frequent the houses of God, which most exegetes take to mean mosques, and who glorify Him there morning and evening. The commentators agree that the trade and sale of these men do not distract them from remembering God, from prayer, or from zakat, and that they put obedience to God before their business. On the meaning of tasbih, Ibn Abbas and others understand it as prayer: the morning refers to the dawn prayer, and the evening to the midday, afternoon and night prayers. Others take it in its literal sense of glorifying God. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Umar and Salim report that the verse was revealed about market traders who leave their dealings at the call to prayer and go to the mosque. On the fear mentioned, some say hearts are agitated by terror, others that they swing between hope of salvation and dread of ruin, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi say that their states change so that hearts understand and eyes see what they had not before. Some explain that men are mentioned because women's prayer at home is better. As for the reward, that God may repay them with their best deeds and give them more of His bounty, some understand it as the multiplication of good deeds.

This verse concludes the description of believers who glorify God in His houses through remembrance and prayer, and it states their aim. The commentators understand that these men do what they do, glorifying God, performing prayer, paying zakat and fearing the Day of Judgment, so that God rewards them with the best of their deeds and adds to them from His bounty beyond what their deeds merit. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi agree that the reward meant is for good deeds, while evil deeds are forgiven for those who obey. Al-Mawardi notes that the extra bounty may mean that a good deed is multiplied tenfold or more, or a gift given without any return. The closing phrase, God provides whom He wills without reckoning, is explained by most as an expression of the vastness and abundance of divine giving, not as a measure. Scholars differ on how the 'so that' clause connects: some attach it to the act of glorifying, others to an implied verb, and Abu al-Baqa' takes it as a lam of result. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan read it as a reward for what they accomplished. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi add that the reward follows the merit of the deeds. The general meaning therefore remains that God's recompense exceeds the measure of their works.

In this verse God describes the deeds of the disbelievers through two images. The first is the mirage in an open plain: the thirsty man takes it for water, but when he reaches it he finds nothing. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that the disbeliever expects his deeds to benefit him, yet on the Day of Resurrection he finds no reward for them, and instead finds God with him, who settles his account. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Razi stress the disappointment and the loss of the expected benefit. The second image is darkness in a deep sea, covered by waves and clouds, which describes the state of the disbeliever in this life. Ibn Abbas and Qatada take the darkness to be his deeds, while Ubayy ibn Ka'b speaks of five darknesses in his words, deeds, entrance, exit and final destiny. Other commentators, such as al-Razi and al-Baydawi, read the sea as the heart, the waves as ignorance and doubt, and the cloud as the seal upon the heart. They differ on the phrase 'he could hardly see it': al-Zajjaj and al-Hasan say he did not see it at all, al-Mubarrad and al-Farra' say he saw it only after great effort, and others say he came close to seeing it but did not. Finally, whoever God does not give light has no light; Ibn Abbas explains this as religion and faith, and al-Zajjaj as guidance. The commentators agree that light and guidance depend on God alone.

This verse tells us that everything in the heavens and on earth glorifies God, and that the birds glorify Him as they spread their wings in flight; each knows its own prayer and glorification, and God knows fully what they do. The commentators agree that tasbih means declaring God free from every defect, but they differ on how it occurs. Mujahid, followed by al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi, holds that prayer (salat) belongs to humans and glorification to the rest of creation, while Sufyan attributes to birds a prayer without bowing or prostration, and al-Naqqash understands their wing-beating as prayer and their song as glorification. On who knows the prayer, al-Zajjaj, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi refer it to God, whereas al-Hasan, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan refer it to each creature itself. Al-Zamakhshari suggests God may inspire birds with their supplication, as He gave them subtle knowledge. Al-Razi argues that the mention of birds shows the power that keeps them aloft and that their glorification is a witness to God rather than speech, while al-Hasan and others see the expression as metaphorical and the majority take it literally. The verse concludes that dominion over the heavens and earth belongs to God and that all things return to Him.

The commentators explain that this verse affirms that absolute sovereignty over the heavens and the earth belongs to God alone: He is the Creator, the Owner and the One who disposes of all things, and all creatures will return to Him after death and resurrection to be judged and repaid for their deeds. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Jalalayn understand sovereignty mainly as authority, governance, provision and the power to judge, while al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy see it as proof that God is the Creator who brings everything into being, and that the final return is to Him. Al-Shawkani and al-Alusi note that attributing ownership to God alone applies both to creation and to the management of beings. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Qasimi connect the verse to what precedes it: since everything belongs to God, guidance and the access to light are also in His hands. The commentators agree that sovereignty and the final return belong to God exclusively, and they raise no disagreement on this point. Al-Sha'rawi and Ibn 'Uthaymin observe that the limited ownership attributed to people elsewhere in the Qur'an is granted by God and does not conflict with His absolute sovereignty. The verse thus calls for fear and hope in God alone and for preparation for the return to Him.

God tells His Prophet that He drives the clouds gently, gathers their scattered pieces until they pile up, and makes rain emerge from their openings. He sends down hail from what the commentators describe as mountains in the sky, striking whom He wills and turning it away from whom He wills, while the flash of His lightning nearly takes away the sight. Most commentators take al-wadq to mean rain and khilal to be the plural of khalal, meaning gaps. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand the hail to come from real mountains of ice in the sky. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy prefer a figurative sense, with the mountains meaning great clouds or abundance. Al-Razi reports both readings and leans toward the literal one as the more apparent. All agree that these signs demonstrate God's power, knowledge and wisdom, and that hail may be a punishment for some and a mercy for others. On sana al-barq, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi say it is the light of the lightning, Qatada links it to its brilliance, and al-Mawardi reports that the sound arises from that brilliance. Abu Ja'far's reading yudhhibu is questioned by al-Akhfash and Abu Hatim, while others defend it as a valid transmission. The alternation of night and day is explained as their succession, as one lengthening at the expense of the other, or as changes of light and darkness. All conclude that these things are a lesson for those with insight.

The commentators read this verse as one of the signs of God's power: He alternates night and day and changes their conditions. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya understand chiefly their succession, one coming after the other, as a lesson for people of insight about God's existence, power and oneness. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and others add that the alternation may mean that one lengthens while the other shortens. Al-Mawardi, al-Nasafi and Ibn al-Jawzi extend the meaning to changes of heat and cold, darkness and light. Al-Nahhas, as cited by al-Qurtubi, understands that the day alternates between the darkness of clouds and the light of the sun, and likewise the night. Al-Mawardi also mentions that the turning may concern what God decrees of good and harm, benefit and injury. Ibn 'Uthaymin holds that the meaning is broader than physical change and includes the reversals of human affairs. The hadith of Abu Hurayra forbidding insults against time, cited by al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and al-Sam'ani, is brought in by some to explain the verse. All agree that the "people of insight" are those whose hearts reflect and draw a lesson. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the emphatic "inna" and the indefinite word "'ibra" address those who, by neglecting reflection, act as though they deny this lesson.

This verse states that God created every creature that crawls or walks on the earth from water. The commentators describe the different ways these creatures move: some go on their bellies, like snakes and fish, some walk on two legs, like humans and birds, and some walk on four, like livestock and beasts. God creates what He wills, and He has power over all things. The exegetes agree that the word dabba refers to every living thing that moves on the ground, and that the use of man for creatures that include non-rational beings follows the rule that the rational are given precedence. They differ on the meaning of water. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi take it to mean the drop of semen, while al-Baghawi, al-Tha'alibi and Ibn 'Ashur report that all creation originates from water, with angels made from wind, jinn from fire and Adam from clay. Al-Qurtubi holds that water is present in the make-up of every animal, and al-Razi offers several answers to the objection that not all creatures come from water. On the reading, al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi note that the variant khaliq kulli dabba is well known and close in meaning to khalaqa. As for moving on the belly, al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur see it as a metaphor or a figure of speech by analogy with those who walk. Some mention a reading attributed to Ubayy, mentioning more than four legs, but Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi do not regard it as Quranic. Finally, al-Razi and al-Nasafi note that the variety of ways of moving, from one common origin, shows God's will and wisdom.

The commentators explain that this verse states that God has sent down clear signs that show the way of truth and right guidance, and that He guides whomever He wills by His grace to the straight path, which is the religion of Islam. Ibn Kathir understands these signs as the clear and firm wisdoms and parables of the Quran, whose understanding is granted to people of intellect and insight. Al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud take guidance to mean being granted the right way of looking at these signs and reflecting on their meanings, and the straight path as the one that leads to the reality of truth and to the reward of Paradise. Al-Razi prefers to read the signs as all the proofs and lessons, since the Quran contains them all, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya link them to the proofs of God's oneness. Most commentators connect the verse to what precedes it, the signs of divine power: the glorification of all creatures in the heavens and on earth, the driving of clouds, and the creation of every living thing from water, so the verse concludes these proofs. Al-Tabari stresses that guidance is a bestowal of God's grace. Ibn Sa'di and al-Sha'rawi add that guidance is given to the one who seeks the truth. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the signs are evident in themselves, yet God alone grants guidance to whom He wills. The commentators thus agree on the clarity of the signs and differ mainly on the scope of divine guidance.

This verse reports the words of the hypocrites: "We believe in Allah and the Messenger, and we obey," and then a group of them turns away afterward, so Allah denies that they are believers. The commentators generally agree that the verse concerns hypocrites whose speech does not match their conduct. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi state that their deeds contradict their words, while al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that true faith requires acceptance and submission, not merely speaking.

They differ on the scope of the denial "and those are not believers." Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi note that it may apply to all who uttered this declaration, so that faith is denied to all of them, or only to the group that turns away, whose earlier profession would then be mere words on the tongue. Ibn 'Ashur holds that the verse addresses hypocrites in general, with a particular group openly refusing the Prophet's judgment.

As for the occasion of revelation, most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi, relate it to a dispute between Bishr, a hypocrite, and a Jew: the Jew wanted to go to the Prophet, while the hypocrite preferred Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf. Al-Mawardi and Ibn 'Ashur report a different version involving al-Mughira ibn Wa'il and 'Ali. Ibn Kathir judges the narration of al-Kalbi to be weak.

Regarding "disease in their hearts," al-Hasan takes it to mean polytheism, while Qatada takes it to mean hypocrisy, and others include both disbelief and hypocrisy. Al-Tabari explains that injustice (al-hayf) means unfair judgment, and that Allah and His Messenger are free of it, while those who turn away are themselves the wrongdoers.

This verse describes hypocrites who profess faith with their tongues and then turn away from obedience. When they are called to God and His Messenger to judge between them, a group of them turns away, though they had just said: we believe and we obey. The commentators explain that this happens when the right is against them; they refuse to be judged by the Prophet. If the right is on their side, they come eagerly and submissively. Scholars differ on the sick hearts: al-Hasan takes it to mean polytheism, Qatada hypocrisy, and some allow that the doubt concerns the Prophet's justice or his prophethood. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that idh'an means hastening in obedience and submission. Al-Mawardi, al-Qurtubi and others report the occasion of revelation: Bishr the hypocrite, who quarrelled with a Jew, or in another version al-Mughira ibn Wa'il and Ali ibn Abi Talib. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan note that the singular pronoun in 'to judge' refers to the Prophet, since his judgement is God's. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-'Arabi draw from the verse the duty to answer a summons to a judge, and Ibn al-'Arabi considers the related hadith weak. The commentators conclude that the verse condemns whoever rejects the judgement of God and His Messenger while knowing the truth.

This verse describes hypocrites who profess faith and obedience with their tongues, yet turn away when they are called to be judged by God and His Messenger. If the right lies with them, they come to him submissive and eager, knowing that he rules with justice. Commentators give the word "mudh'inin" closely related meanings: obedient, hastening, submissive, or acquiescent. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi agree that this submission does not reflect acceptance of the ruling but a preference for their own desires: they seek justice when it favours them and avoid it when it does not. Al-Tabari adds that the word "kana" does not report a past event but serves as a rebuke and a lesson. Accounts of the occasion of revelation differ: al-Mawardi, al-Wahidi and Muqatil relate the story of Bishr the hypocrite and his Jewish opponent, while al-Mawardi also mentions a version involving al-Mughira ibn Wa'il and Ali, and they agree on the blameworthy conduct. Scholars differ on the "disease in the hearts": al-Hasan takes it as polytheism, Qatada as hypocrisy, and al-Razi reads it as a gradual hypocrisy. Ibn Ashur clarifies that the verse targets hypocrites who display faith. Al-Qurtubi derives from it the duty to answer a summons to a judge, while Ibn al-Arabi regards the related hadith as weak.

This passage describes hypocrites who profess faith and obedience with their tongues, then turn away when they are called to be judged by the judgment of God and His Messenger. The commentators explain that the verse rebukes this refusal and asks about its cause. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir understand it as the hypocrites' refusal to appeal to the Prophet ﷺ when the right is against them, while they hasten to him when the right is theirs. Al-Hasan and Qatada take the 'sickness' in the heart to mean polytheism or hypocrisy. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy present three possibilities, a sickness of the heart, doubt about the prophethood, or fear of injustice in the judgment, and the verse dismisses the third with 'rather, they are the wrongdoers'. Al-Razi holds that the doubt arose after Islam had settled in the heart, while Ibn 'Ashur describes these people as having confessed Islam with their tongues without inward conviction. The verse then sets against them the true words of believers, 'we hear and we obey', on which the commentators agree. They differ over the following verse about oaths and 'known obedience': al-Zamakhshari sees it as better than false oaths, while Mujahid takes it to mean obedience in words alone. Ibn Kathir concludes that faith is not mere speech. He also cites a mursal hadith from al-Hasan that counts as a wrongdoer whoever refuses to answer the summons to a Muslim judge, which Ibn al-'Arabi considers baseless and Ibn 'Atiyya does not accept.

This verse describes how believers should respond when they are called to the judgment of God and His Messenger. The commentators explain that it is not a report of a past event but a lesson in conduct: the believer should say, 'We hear and we obey.' They agree that the call refers to the Book of God and the Prophet's judgment, that obedience covers both action and speech, and that success (falah) means attaining what one seeks and being saved from what one fears. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that the verse was revealed about a hypocrite named Bishr who, in a dispute with a Jew, refused to go to the Prophet and preferred Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf. Al-Mawardi mentions another report involving al-Mughira ibn Wa'il and 'Ali, but the first account is the most widely cited. Most scholars take the judgment to belong to the Messenger, since he conveys God's command. On grammar, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Nasafi prefer the accusative for 'qawl', which they judge stronger than the nominative, and note the passive reading 'liyuhkama'. Al-Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir, al-Shawkani and al-Alusi point out that refusal may stem from hypocrisy, sickness of the heart or doubt, and that the Prophet's rulings were accepted by the sincere. Ibn 'Uthaymin holds that the verse describes a constant attitude of the believer, and that refusal of the truth arises from a sick heart, doubt or fear of injustice.

The commentators explain that this verse gathers the causes of success: whoever obeys God and His Messenger in what they command and forbid, fears God for past sins and guards himself against them in the future, these are the winners, meaning those saved from the Fire and admitted to Paradise. There is broad agreement that obedience covers both doing what is commanded and avoiding what is forbidden, and that awe and piety are acts of worship owed to God alone. Ibn 'Abbas, as transmitted by al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, assigns obedience to the obligations and recommended practices, fear to past sins, and piety to what remains of life. Ibn 'Ashur distinguishes fear, which concerns duties neglected in the past, from piety, which is the careful avoidance of violations in the future. The verse belongs to a passage criticising hypocrites who turn away when called to God's judgment; al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi mention a dispute between a hypocrite and a Jew as the occasion, and note that believers answer "We hear and we obey". The readers differ in pronouncing the final vowels of "wa yattaqhi", and al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi explain that these are accepted shortened forms in Arabic. Al-Tha'alibi and Ibn Kathir add reports urging obedience, and Ibn 'Uthaymin stresses that success is reserved for those who combine these qualities.

This passage describes hypocrites who swear by God with the strongest oaths that they will go out if the Prophet ﷺ orders them to, and the reply forbids such swearing. According to the commentators, the verse was revealed about hypocrites who promised the Prophet complete obedience, and the Qur'an exposes the falseness of their promise. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy generally understand the going out as going out to fight, while Ibn 'Atiyya holds that it may also mean leaving one's wealth and homes, a reading Ibn 'Ashur also records. The phrase 'known obedience' is read in several ways: Mujahid, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it to mean that their obedience is known to be mere words and lies; al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud take it as an obedience that is well known and beyond doubt; al-Zajjaj and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that it is better than false oaths. Al-Mawardi offers a reading in which their hypocrisy is already known. The commentators also stress that God knows both what is hidden and what is shown, and will hold them to account for their deeds.

God commands His Prophet to tell both believers and hypocrites: obey God and obey the Messenger. If you turn away, the Messenger bears only what he was charged with, and you bear what you were charged with; if you obey him, you will be guided, and the Messenger's duty is only the clear delivery of the message.
