The commentators link this verse to the hypocrites who swore solemnly that they would go out to fight if commanded; God replies that their known obedience is a lie and that He knows what they do. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir understand turning away as refusing to obey God and His Messenger, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi hold that the harm of turning away falls only on those who turn away. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan discuss the verb form of 'tawallaw', which most take as an elision of 'tatawallaw'. Al-Mawardi reads the 'clear delivery' as words for those who obey and the sword for those who disobey, whereas most restrict it to plain transmission. All agree that guidance is tied to obeying the Prophet, and there is no major disagreement over the meaning of the verse itself.

This verse promises those among the believers who combine faith with righteous deeds that Allah will make them successors on earth, as He made successors of those before them, will establish for them the religion He has approved, and will change their fear into security so that they worship Him without associating anything with Him. Whoever disbelieves after this is among the defiantly disobedient. The commentators report that it was revealed while the Muslims lived in fear. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that inheriting the land means ruling the lands of unbelievers, as was granted to the Children of Israel after the tyrants were destroyed, that establishing the religion means making it firm and dominant, and that the change from fear to security came after the migration and the conquest of the Arabian Peninsula. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi report that the disbelief meant is ingratitude for the blessing rather than disbelief in God, while Ibn 'Atiyya allows both meanings. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi extend the promise to the whole community, and some scholars cite it as evidence for the legitimacy of the rightly guided caliphs, while others limit it to other contexts. Al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi give several views on the land promised, which some identify as Mecca and others as the lands of Arabs and non-Arabs. Readers differ on the vocalisation of two words, and al-Tabari considers the intensified form more correct. On the phrase "they worship Me", Mujahid explains it as "they love none but Me" and Ibn 'Abbas as "they fear none but Me". Ibn 'Ashur sees in the verse a promise of social stability conditioned on faith and good deeds.

This verse commands believers to establish prayer, pay zakat and obey the Messenger ﷺ, in the hope of receiving God's mercy. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that these acts are to be performed in hope of mercy, and Ibn Kathir adds that whoever does so will surely be shown mercy. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi connect the word "so that" to the three commands together, or to the last one only. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi hold that the repetition of the command to obey the Messenger serves to emphasise its obligation, and that the prayer and zakat may be linked to "obey God" even with a separating phrase in between. The next sentence, "Let not those who disbelieved think they can escape on earth", was read by most with the second-person form addressed to the Prophet, while Ibn 'Amir and Hamza read it in the third person. The commentators explain that the disbelievers cannot escape God, and that their refuge is the Fire. Ibn 'Ashur notes that these commands are addressed specifically to believers, distinct from the call to the disbelievers that precedes them. The exegetes present these readings without choosing between them.

The commentators explain that the verse addresses the Prophet ﷺ and means that no one should suppose those who disbelieved can escape God on earth, however powerful or numerous they are; they will surely be overtaken, and their abode is the Fire, a wretched destination. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi stress that God is able to destroy them, and that delay is not neglect, a point echoed by al-Sa'di. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur observe that the verb 'tahsabanna' takes two objects, so 'mu'jizina fi al-ard' serves as both in the second-person reading; al-Zamakhshari reads it as meaning that no one can render God powerless on earth. For the third-person reading, attributed to Ibn 'Amir and Hamza, the grammarians offered several analyses, with the subject either 'those who disbelieved' or the Prophet; al-Farra' and Abu Hayyan judged it weak without rejecting it. The exegetes agree that 'wa ma'wahum al-nar' is coordinated with the prohibition in a declarative sense, and al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi note that the lam in 'labi'sa' introduces an implied oath. Ibn 'Ashur adds that naming the Fire as dwelling and final destination heightens the solemnity of the statement.

This verse tells believers to instruct their slaves and young children who have not reached puberty to ask permission before entering their rooms at three times: before the dawn prayer, when people take off their night clothes, at midday when they undress for the afternoon rest, and after the night prayer. These are times when people are undressed and their nakedness may be exposed, which is why the verse calls them three 'awrat', moments of nakedness. At other times there is no blame in entering without permission, because these people come and go constantly to serve the household, and asking every time would be a burden on them and on the family. Ibn 'Umar takes the command to refer to men only, al-Sulami to women only, while most commentators include both sexes; Ibn 'Abbas also applies it to men and women. Scholars differ on whether the ruling still stands. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Ibn Jubayr held it abrogated, while al-Sha'bi said it was not abrogated and that people had simply neglected it. Ibn 'Abbas, as Ibn Kathir reports, regarded it as binding but tied to a time when houses had no doors or curtains. Most scholars read the command as an obligation, whereas Abu Qilaba understood it as a recommendation. Once a child reaches puberty, they must ask permission at all times, like adults. As for elderly women past childbearing who no longer hope for marriage, they may set aside their outer garments, such as the outer cloak or veil, provided they do not display adornment, and it is better for them to remain modest. The verse closes by noting that God is all-knowing and wise in what He makes clear.

This verse teaches that free children who have not yet reached puberty must ask permission before entering at three times: before the dawn prayer, when people take off their clothes at midday, and after the night prayer, because these are times of undress and privacy, which the text calls three nakednesses. Outside these times, children and servants may enter without permission, since they move around the household serving its members. Once a child reaches puberty, he must ask permission at all times, like the adults. The commentators agree that puberty is reached through nocturnal emission, and differ on other signs.

Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that "those before them" are the adult men of the family, while al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi take them to be the adult men mentioned earlier in the surah. Ibn Abbas said most people did not act on this verse, while al-Sha'bi and Sa'id ibn Jubayr held that it is not abrogated. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib considered it abrogated. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi accept that the command is binding, even for a son toward his mother, as Ibn Mas'ud said. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the majority regard the command as obligatory, whereas Abu Qilaba read it as a recommendation.

Jurists differ on the age of puberty when no emission occurs: Abu Hanifa sets it at eighteen for boys and seventeen for girls, while al-Shafi'i, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad set it at fifteen, and al-Razi examines these positions. In the second part, elderly women who no longer hope for marriage may set aside their outer garments without displaying adornment, though modesty is better for them, according to most commentators.

This verse addresses al-qawa'id, elderly women who have passed the age of childbearing and menstruation and no longer hope for marriage. The commentators, from al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir to al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy, agree that God permits them to set aside their outer garments, such as the jilbab, the rida or the cover placed over the khimar, provided they do not display adornment to attract attention. Most define tabarruj as the forced display of what should be concealed, and the adornment meant here is the hidden kind. The phrase that restraint is better for them means that refraining from removing these garments is preferable, even though removing them is allowed. Al-Zamakhshari observes that this shows that removing garments has no bearing on chastity.

Scholars differ on what "garments" means. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr take it to mean the jilbab or rida worn over the khimar, while Jabir ibn Zayd includes the khimar itself. Al-Baghawi reports that Ibn 'Abbas forbade removing the khimar. Some readings, attributed to Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy ibn Ka'b, read "some of their garments", which narrows the sense. Ibn Kathir notes that the permission to uncover the head or hair is not unanimously accepted, and al-Qurtubi holds that an elderly woman is in principle bound by the same modesty as a young one, except regarding the outer jilbab.

Ibn 'Ashur, al-Sha'rawi and Ibn 'Uthaymin stress that this concession depends on the absence of any risk of temptation. Ibn 'Uthaymin adds that the ruling follows its underlying reason and that it is wiser to keep away from anything that could raise suspicion.

This verse lifts the burden of blame from the blind, the lame and the sick, meaning there is no sin on them for what their condition prevents them from doing. It then permits believers to eat from the houses of their children, parents, brothers and sisters, paternal and maternal uncles and aunts, from houses entrusted to their care, or from the homes of close friends. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand the lifting of blame as relating to eating together: some Muslims avoided sharing meals with these people, or feared taking others' property in their absence. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi report the various opinions on the occasion of revelation, while al-Tabari prefers to follow the apparent meaning of the text without committing to one story. Eating together or separately is permitted, though Ibn Kathir notes that eating as a group carries more blessing. As for the greeting, most exegetes, including al-Tabari and Ibn Juzayy, understand that on entering a house one greets its occupants; if no one is present, one says: peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of God. Ibn Kathir and al-Alusi state that this greeting comes from God, and it is blessed and good. Ibn Juzayy and al-Qasimi add that it brings peace and blessings.

This verse describes true believers as those who, when they are with the Prophet ﷺ on a common matter, such as fighting, Friday prayer or a general consultation, do not leave until they have asked his leave. If they ask for permission for a legitimate reason, he may grant it to whomever he wishes, and God forgives them. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read this as a rule of conduct toward the leader of the community, and Ibn Kathir adds that whoever keeps it is among the perfect believers. On the meaning of a common matter, opinions differ. Ibn Zayd and Ibn Sallam take it mainly as war or prayer with a sermon, while al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and others take it as any collective obedience. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi stress that leaving without permission is a grave fault, close to hypocrisy, whereas al-Baydawi says that asking permission is itself a sign of faith. The decision to grant or refuse is left to the Prophet's judgement about the public interest. Qatada holds that this ruling was abrogated by a verse of al-Tawba, which other commentators do not accept. Ibn al-Arabi, cited by al-Qurtubi, restricts the rule to war, while the broader reading is preferred. Several exegetes connect the following verses, which forbid calling the Prophet by his bare name and condemn those who slip away from the assembly under cover, to the same theme of respect.

The commentators explain that this verse teaches believers how to treat the Prophet ﷺ with respect, both in how they address him and in how they ask leave to depart from his gatherings. The most widely shared reading is that God forbids calling him as people call one another, such as "O Muhammad," and instructs them to say "O Prophet of God" or "O Messenger of God," in a gentle and reverent tone. Ibn Abbas, as reported by al-Tabari, understood the verse differently, as a warning not to provoke the Prophet, since his supplication against someone is answered. Al-Tabari prefers the view of Ibn Abbas, because the verses before and after concern leaving without permission and the threat that follows.

The commentators agree that those who slip away from the gathering, sheltering behind one another, are hypocrites who leave secretly. According to various reports, this happened during the Friday sermon, during the digging of the trench, or in battle, where Mujahid understood it as withdrawing from the ranks. Al-Farra and al-Zajjaj explain that lawadh means taking cover.

As for those who oppose his command, Ibn Kathir and others read it as the command of the Prophet or of God, while al-Akhfash treats the particle "an" as superfluous and others read in it the sense of turning away. On the meaning of fitna, Ibn Abbas says killing, Mujahid a trial in this world, al-Suddi disbelief, and al-Hasan the revelation of hidden hypocrisy. The painful punishment is placed by some in this life and by others in the next.

Jurists have drawn from this verse that a command implies obligation, since God threatens those who oppose it. Other scholars, such as Ibn Ashur, take amr here to mean affair or conduct, which changes the force of that argument.

This closing verse affirms that all that is in the heavens and the earth belongs to God alone, that He knows people's inner and outer condition, whether faith, hypocrisy, obedience or disobedience, and that on the day they return to Him He will inform them of their deeds and repay them, for He has knowledge of everything. Most commentators read it as a reminder of God's dominion and knowledge, which should lead believers to fear disobeying His command. They agree that the return to God means the Day of Resurrection. They differ, however, on who is addressed. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take the address to be general to all people, while al-Razi, al-Nasafi, Ibn Juzayy and al-Baydawi hold that "the day they are returned" refers to the hypocrites, or that the address shifts to them. Most read "qad" here as emphasis that confirms the threat; al-Zamakhshari explains that it strengthens the warning, and Ibn Uthaymin also takes it as affirmation, whereas the two Jalals note that it can sometimes signal diminution. Ibn 'Ashur sees the verse as a general conclusion to the whole surah and explains that "what you are upon" covers both good and bad states. Ibn Kathir stresses that God's report covers small and great deeds alike. The commentators agree that "what you are upon" includes faith, hypocrisy, obedience and disobedience, though some restrict it to hypocrisy in this context. The shared meaning is that God owns everything, knows everything, and will call His servants to account on the Day of Resurrection.
